question: What visualization techniques and tool families were available for explaining recurrent and Transformer language models, what parts of the model lifecycle did they expose, and where did visualization still fall short as an explanation?

key_findings.claim: The survey separates general model-agnostic explanation dashboards from language-model-specific visual systems and argues that each serves a different debugging workflow.
key_findings.evidence: Model-agnostic tools such as LIME, SHAP, TensorBoard, and experiment dashboards emphasize reusable attribution and metrics, while specialized systems expose attention heads, hidden states, embeddings, corpora, or token-level information flow. The paper presents transferability versus depth of inspection as the central trade-off.

key_findings.claim: Transformer visualization work is organized into focused views of one mechanism and holistic systems that attempt to cover the model lifecycle.
key_findings.evidence: Focused tools predominantly use attention maps, embedding projections, probing plots, and attribution charts. The holistic comparison records which systems cover corpora, embeddings, heads, attention, neurons, layers, inputs, and outputs, and concludes that none covers all facets.

key_findings.claim: The review warns that attention visualization is not automatically a faithful causal explanation.
key_findings.evidence: The Transformer section notes the active debate over whether attention weights explain predictions and treats attention maps as only one view among probing, hidden-state, corpus, and output analyses. This caveat limits any inference from visual salience to model reasoning.

key_findings.claim: The proposed future direction is a reusable component system that summarizes and compares multiple levels from training corpora through model outputs.
key_findings.evidence: The conclusion calls for components specialized to corpora, embeddings, attention heads, and task-specific layers, with summaries at neuron, layer, input, and output levels plus comparison across model settings. This is a design agenda, not an empirically evaluated interface specification.

method.core_idea: Synthesize language-model visualization work through a qualitative taxonomy of model-agnostic tools, recurrent-network views, focused Transformer views, holistic Transformer systems, and multimodal extensions.
method.mechanism: The authors select cited systems and papers, describe their visualization subjects and chart types, and compare coverage in tables spanning corpora, embeddings, hidden states, attention, neurons, layers, inputs, outputs, and evaluation. The synthesis then identifies recurring interface patterns and missing lifecycle coverage.
assumptions: Citation prominence and the authors' selection process capture the practically important visualization landscape.
Tool feature coverage and chart taxonomy are useful proxies for explanation utility.
RNN and Transformer visualization patterns can be compared despite different architectures and research objectives.
Visual inspection contributes to understanding even when causal faithfulness is not established.

techniques.role: Compares which lifecycle components holistic tools expose.
Separates mechanism-specific plots from integrated model-analysis environments.
Connects language-model analysis targets to heatmaps, projections, parallel coordinates, graphs, and linked views.
Frames explanation as tracing problems from corpus and embeddings through internal layers to outputs.

evaluations.setting: Qualitative comparison of RNN visualization papers
evaluations.metric: Coverage of visualization subject and chart type
evaluations.result: Hidden-state dynamics, saliency heatmaps, embeddings, and neuron activations recur across systems.
evaluations.baseline: Narrative comparison rather than a controlled user study

evaluations.setting: Focused and holistic Transformer visualization systems
evaluations.metric: Coverage of corpus, embeddings, heads, attention, neurons, layers, inputs, and outputs
evaluations.result: BertViz, VisBERT, exBERT, AttViz, and related tools cover different subsets; no reviewed system spans the full lifecycle.

limitations: The search and inclusion protocol is narrative rather than systematic, so coverage and reproducibility are uncertain.
The paper compares features and chart types but reports no user study, task completion time, error rate, or faithfulness benchmark.
The fast-moving survey is centered on pre-2022 tools and predates widespread instruction-tuned and multimodal foundation models.
Visualization can communicate correlations or salience without demonstrating a causal mechanism.
Tool availability, maintenance status, and reproducibility are not audited consistently.
failure_modes: Users can read attention or gradient heatmaps as causal explanations when they are not faithful.
Dense linked views can create an illusion of completeness while omitting data provenance, counterfactuals, or uncertainty.
Model-specific tools can become obsolete as architectures change, while generic dashboards may be too shallow for diagnosis.
Cherry-picked examples and visually appealing patterns can substitute for quantitative validation.
reusable_insights: Design atlas views around user questions and lifecycle stages, not merely around available model tensors.
Pair every salience visualization with a faithfulness caveat or intervention-based check.
Use coordinated overview-and-detail views so corpus distributions, model internals, and individual examples can be traced together.
Make cross-model comparison and summarization first-class rather than forcing one-model-at-a-time inspection.
open_questions: Which visual encodings measurably improve debugging accuracy for modern foundation models?
How should uncertainty, causal interventions, and counterfactual validity be represented alongside attention and attribution?
Can a stable intermediate data model let visualization components survive rapid architecture changes?
What lifecycle views are most useful for retrieval-augmented, tool-using, and multimodal language models?

competitive_landscape.title: A Multiscale Visualization of Attention in the Transformer Model
competitive_landscape.difference: BertViz supplies interactive head, model, and neuron views for Transformer attention; the reviewed paper does not propose a new tool but positions BertViz within a broader lifecycle and visualization taxonomy.

competitive_landscape.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
competitive_landscape.difference: exBERT links corpus examples, contextual embeddings, and attention patterns for interactive exploration. The survey uses it as evidence for holistic analysis while noting that no system covers every lifecycle facet.

competitive_landscape.title: The Language Interpretability Tool: Extensible, Interactive Visualizations and Analysis for NLP Models
competitive_landscape.difference: LIT provides an extensible platform integrating salience, counterfactuals, embeddings, metrics, and example exploration; it operationalizes much of the survey's reusable-component agenda more concretely than the survey's descriptive tables.

competitive_landscape.title: Attention is not Explanation
competitive_landscape.difference: Jain and Wallace empirically show that attention distributions can be weakly related to gradient importance and can be changed without altering predictions. This directly constrains the explanatory interpretation of attention maps cataloged by the survey.

novelty_assessment: The paper's value is a broad, visualization-centered synthesis of language-model tools and a focused-versus-holistic taxonomy, not a new explanation algorithm or validated interface. Earlier XAI surveys, BertViz, exBERT, and LIT already establish many components; the distinctive contribution is gathering RNN, Transformer, model-agnostic, and multimodal visualization practices into one design-oriented account.
reviewer_notes: Read the full extracted survey including selection discussion, RNN and Transformer taxonomies, Tables 1-4, discussion, and conclusion. Competitor/tool papers were checked on their primary arXiv records on 2026-08-23. Because this is a narrative survey, conclusions about utility are separated from the paper's descriptive evidence.
